name: Bamu Kiwai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1973. The Kiwaian language family. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea, 217-260. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C26.217 (open access, sealang.net PL edition).
catalog_locator: p.226, sec. 6.51 'Phonology' (family-level); p.242, sec. 6.63.4 'Notes on Bamu Kiwai'; pp.249-250, North-Eastern Kiwai notes.
catalog_quote: [p.226] The suprasegmental systems are relatively complicated and manifest themselves in complex stress systems with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system is present in all the languages, except apparently in Wabuda. Its functional load appears to be low in all the languages except for North-Eastern Kiwai and (Arigibi ?) where it seems to be quite high. The syllable structures are very simple; no consonant clusters occur (except for the very rare presence of -nd- in Kerewo) and all syllables are open. [p.242] In other respects, Bamu Kiwai phonology is much more like that of other Kiwaian languages than that of Wabuda. Long vowels are rare, and a two-tone system appears to be present. [pp.249-250, on North-Eastern Kiwai] ... the two-tone system which is a feature of the Kiwaian languages except for Wabuda (see 6.51.) seems to have a much higher functional load than the low one observable in other Kiwaian languages (except perhaps for Arigibi, see 6.67.). Stress features yet to be studied in detail in North-Eastern Kiwai and the other Kiwaian languages may play a part in this.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (44 pp., sealang.net/Pacific Linguistics open-access edition, CC BY-SA 4.0; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Chapter 6: The Kiwaian Language Family', author S.A. Wurm) and re-extracted PDF pages 10 and 25-26 with extracted text, then viewed the saved page scan and. Both quoted passages are there word for word. p.226, sec. 6.51 'Phonology' (under 6.5 'Typological and Structural Features of Kiwaian Languages'): 'The suprasegmental systems are relatively complicated and manifest themselves in complex stress systems with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system is present in all the languages, except apparently in Wabuda. Its functional load appears to be low in all the languages except…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress placement is given. Wurm's survey says every Kiwaian language including Bamu Kiwai has a 'complex stress system with rhythm patterns' plus a two-tone system of low functional load, and specifically that Bamu Kiwai 'appears' to have a two-tone system; the position of word stress is not stated anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only 'rhythm patterns' at family level).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Bamu; Wabuda is said to lack the two-tone system; tone has high functional load in North-Eastern Kiwai (and Arigibi?).
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level typological summary (sec. 6.51) explicitly covering all Kiwaian languages; the Bamu-specific paragraph (sec. 6.63.4) is based on Ray 1923, Wurm 1951, Capell 1962, Riley & Ray 1930-31, Voorhoeve's Middle Bamu materials and Wurm's own Sisiame field notes. Word-level phonology; no phrase/citation-form distinction discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Bamu = Bamu Kiwai (Glottolog bamu1257, ISO bcf), which Wurm 1973 (sec. 6.63) divides into Sisiame (main, c. 2,850 speakers), Pirupiru/Gama (c. 850) and Middle Bamu (c. 700; the mission standard, Scripture 1952) dialects; Riley & Ray's vocabularies are Sisiame (with Oropai) and Pirupiru, Ray 1913-14 has Sisiami and Buniki (= Dibiri), Wurm's own notes are Sisiame, and the Carr & Carr dictionary labels forms Odi / Humo. The quoted p.226 statement is a family-level generalisation over all Kiwaian languages; only the p.242 tone sentence is Bamu-specific.
